title: TRUE or FALSE? 12 Animal Facts That Were Never True (Disney Faked One)

beats.say: Last time I promised you Disney, a cliff, and a very fake documentary. Today you get that, plus eleven more animal facts that are completely made up.
Stick around to the end, because one of these was faked by people who won an Oscar for it.
Let's play. Before each one, you get three seconds to guess true or false. Keep score, and tell me your number out of twelve in the comments.
beats.text:
GUESS TRUE
OR FALSE.
KEEP SCORE.

beats.say: True or false? Lemmings jump off cliffs together.
Lemmings do not jump off cliffs. Not to save the planet, not because they're sad, not ever. And the reason everybody thinks they do is a Disney movie.
Lemmings are these chubby little rodents that live up in the Arctic tundra. Basically a hamster that got really into camping.
Every few years their numbers explode. Lots of food, lots of babies, and suddenly the tundra is packed.
So a lot of them head out looking for somewhere less crowded. They move, they spread out, and some even try to swim across rivers and lakes.
Some don't make it across. That's it. That's the whole story. No group suicide. No tiny lemming cult.
Then in nineteen fifty eight, Disney released a nature documentary called White Wilderness. And it showed lemmings running off a cliff into the sea.
Here's the problem. According to a Canadian TV investigation years later, the lemmings were bought and shipped in, and the 'migration' shots were filmed on a spinning turntable covered in snow.
And for the big cliff scene, the crew herded them over the edge themselves. The narrator just called it nature.
That movie won the Oscar for best documentary. So the most famous lemming fact on Earth came from a film crew, not from lemmings.
Real lemmings, by the way, are doing fine. They just want to eat moss and be left alone. Honestly, relatable.
True or false? Camels store water in their humps.
beats.quiz:
CAMELS STORE
WATER IN
THEIR HUMPS

beats.say: Camels do not store water in their humps. If you cut one open, which please don't, you would not find a fish tank.
The hump is fat. A big lump of fat, sometimes dozens of kilos of it.
When food runs out, the camel burns that fat for energy, and the hump actually shrinks and flops over to the side, like a sad deflated beanbag.
So where does the water go? Mostly into their blood and body tissue. Camels can lose a huge share of their body water and keep walking, when that would knock most mammals out.
And when they finally find water, they don't sip. A thirsty camel can drink over a hundred liters in about ten minutes.
Keeping fat in one lump on top also helps them stay cool. If that fat were spread all over the body like a blanket, they'd overheat in the desert.
beats.text:
FAT ON TOP =
COOL EVERYWHERE
ELSE

beats.say: So the hump isn't a canteen. It's a lunchbox.
True or false? Porcupines can shoot their quills.
Porcupines cannot shoot their quills. Cartoons lied to you again.
A North American porcupine has around thirty thousand quills, and each one is just loosely attached to the skin.
When something gets too close, the porcupine raises the quills, turns its back, and swings its tail. Touch it, and the quills pop right out into you.
Each tip is covered in tiny backward barbs, so they go in easy and come out terrible.
But the porcupine has to actually make contact. It can't fire them across the room like a crossbow. And don't worry about the porcupine, it grows new ones.
So the rule is simple. Don't touch the porcupine. The porcupine has been very clear about this.
True or false? Daddy longlegs are the most venomous spiders.
You've probably heard that daddy longlegs are the most venomous creatures in the world, but their fangs are too short to bite you. Two problems with that.
Problem one. The thing most people call a daddy longlegs is a harvestman. And a harvestman isn't even a spider.
It has one round body instead of two sections, it doesn't make silk, and it has no venom glands at all. Zero venom. It's a tiny walking button with stilts.
Problem two. People also call the skinny cellar spider in your basement a daddy longlegs. That one does have venom, but it's weak, and there's no evidence it's dangerous to people.
When MythBusters tested it, the spider's fangs could actually get into skin, and the host said it felt like a tiny burning sensation that went away in seconds.
So not the most venomous. Not even close. Just a very leggy roommate.
True or false? Owls can turn their heads all the way around.
Owls cannot spin their heads all the way around. They can turn it about two hundred seventy degrees, which is still completely terrifying.
They need to, because owl eyes are shaped more like tubes than balls. They can't roll them around in their sockets like we can. So the whole head has to move.
To make that work, an owl has fourteen neck bones. You have seven.
They also have special blood vessels and little blood reservoirs in the neck, so twisting all the way around doesn't cut off blood to the brain.
If you tried that, you would not be looking behind you. You'd be looking at the ceiling of an ambulance.
Two hundred seventy degrees, not three sixty. Close, but the full spin is a horror movie thing.
True or false? Elephants drink through their trunks like a straw.
Elephants do not drink through their trunks like a straw. If they did, it would be the world's longest milkshake.
What they actually do is suck water partway up the trunk, hold it there, then curl the trunk back and squirt it into their mouth.
An adult African elephant can hold several liters of water in its trunk at once.
And that trunk is a nose and an upper lip fused together, packed with tens of thousands of muscles and no bones at all.
It can pick up a single peanut, rip a branch off a tree, or give its baby a shower. Your nose can't do any of that.
True or false? Chameleons change color to hide.
Chameleons don't change color mainly to blend in. That's the most famous thing about them, and it's mostly wrong.
Their normal resting colors already match the trees pretty well. The big color shows are usually about communication.
A male panther chameleon puts on his brightest colors to show off to females and to tell other males to back off.
They also shift darker to soak up heat when they're cold, and lighter when they're warm.
And the way they do it is wild. A lot of the color comes from tiny crystals in their skin cells. The chameleon changes the spacing between them, and that changes how light bounces off.
So a chameleon going bright isn't saying hide me. It's saying look at me.
beats.text:
NOT HIDE ME.
LOOK AT ME.

beats.say: True or false? Hippos sweat blood.
Hippos do not sweat blood. Even though it really, really looks like they do.
Their skin oozes a thick liquid that starts out clear and turns red, then brown. So people looked at a hippo dripping red and assumed the worst.
It's not blood, and it's not really sweat either. Scientists think it works like a built-in sunscreen and may help fight off germs too.
Which makes sense, because hippos spend all day in hot sun and muddy water. Imagine if your body just made its own SPF.
Hippos are still one of the most dangerous animals in Africa, though. So, sunscreen yes, hugs no.
True or false? If you touch a baby bird, its mom will abandon it.
beats.quiz:
TOUCH A BABY
BIRD = MOM
LEAVES IT

beats.say: If you touch a baby bird, its mom will NOT smell you and abandon it. Your grandma meant well, but no.
Most songbirds have a pretty weak sense of smell. They're not sniffing their kids for human fingerprints.
And parent birds put a ton of work into their babies. They're not giving up on one because it got touched.

Also, a lot of 'abandoned' baby birds aren't abandoned at all. Fluffy babies with feathers hopping around on the ground are fledglings, and that's a normal stage. Mom and dad are usually nearby, still feeding them.
So the best move is usually to leave it alone and keep your cat inside. If it's a tiny bald nestling and you can see the nest, you can gently put it back.
beats.text:
LEAVE IT.
KEEP THE CAT IN.

beats.say: True or false? Sloths are lazy.
And finally, sloths are not lazy. They're on the most extreme budget in the animal kingdom.
Sloths eat leaves, and leaves have almost no energy in them. Digesting one meal can take days, sometimes weeks.
So they save energy everywhere. They move slowly, they have an unusually low body temperature for a mammal, and they blend into the trees so they don't have to run from anything.
They only climb down about once a week, and it's to go to the bathroom. That's the big trip.
Fun bonus fact. Sloths are surprisingly good swimmers. Slow on land, decent in the pool.
So they're not lazy. They're just the most efficient animal you know.
True or false? Koalas are bears.
Koalas are not bears. Calling it a koala bear is like calling a cat a dog because it has four legs.
Koalas are marsupials. Their closest living relatives are wombats, and a baby koala, called a joey, grows up in its mom's pouch, like a kangaroo.
Early European settlers in Australia saw a round, fluffy, tree-climbing thing and went, eh, close enough, bear. And the name stuck for two hundred years.
They also eat almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves, which are tough, low in energy, and pretty toxic to most animals.
To save energy, koalas spend most of the day, up to around twenty hours, resting or asleep.
beats.text:
UP TO ~20 HOURS
OF REST A DAY

beats.say: So the sloth earlier? Not lazy. The koala? Okay, that one's a little bit lazy. But it's not a bear.
True or false? Bees always die after they sting you.
All bees die after they sting you. Nope. Most of them can sting again.
The ones that die are worker honeybees, and mainly when they sting something with thick, stretchy skin, like you.
Their stinger has tiny backward barbs. In skin like ours it gets stuck, and when the bee pulls away, the stinger stays behind. The bee doesn't survive that.
But when a honeybee stings another insect, the stinger can usually slide back out, and the bee flies off fine.
Bumblebees and wasps have smooth stingers, so they can sting you over and over. And male bees? They can't sting at all. Zero weapons. Just vibes.
So that bee isn't on a suicide mission. It's just having a really bad day because of your arm.
beats.text:
NOT A MISSION.
A BAD DAY.

beats.say: Okay, scores. Every single one was false. If you got twelve out of twelve, I don't believe you. Drop your real score in the comments, and tell me which one got you.
And if you want part three, subscribe, because next time we're going after sharks, goldfish bowls, and the alligator living in the sewer.
